meta.title: Who really said "Never write an advertisement which you wouldn't want your own family to read"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — David Ogilvy, in Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963). It is one of his rules, and the three sentences after it are the argument.

answer.sourceLine: Ogilvy set this down as one of his rules in Confessions of an Advertising Man (Atheneum, 1963). Quote Investigator ↗ places it in chapter 5, page 99, and says it verified that page against a hardcopy; Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ transcribes the same passage from the Ballantine paperback at page 87.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 99 (Atheneum hardcopy, per Quote Investigator); 87 in the Ballantine paperback, per Wikiquote
A numbered rule, set as a heading, with its reasoning beneath

source.excerpt: Never Write an Advertisement Which You Wouldn’t Want Your Own Family To Read. You wouldn’t tell lies to your own wife. Don’t tell them to mine. Do as you would be done by.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to Confessions of an Advertising Man, chapter 5, page 99, Atheneum, New York, 1963, and states the page was verified against a hardcopy. It records no earlier appearance and no other claimant.

Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ carries the rule and the three sentences that follow it, citing the same book at page 87 of the Ballantine edition. Different printing, different pagination, same wording.
Wikipedia ↗ confirms the book: Atheneum, August 1963, structured as an eleven-chapter playbook of more than two hundred rules. This sentence is one of them.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of the 1963 Atheneum edition ↗, but it is lending-restricted and its full text is not searchable from here, so we could not confirm page 99 independently.
source.excerptNote: The rule is set in title case in the book, as a heading, and the three sentences beneath it are its argument. This is the passage as Quote Investigator ↗ and Wikiquote ↗ both transcribe it. We could not open the book ourselves — the Internet Archive’s scan of the 1963 Atheneum edition is lending-restricted — so the page numbers are theirs, not ours.

author.heading: About David Ogilvy
author.metaLine: 1911–1999 · British advertising executive, founder of Ogilvy & Mather
author.bio: David Mackenzie Ogilvy founded his advertising agency in New York in 1948 with $6,000 and financial backing from his brother Francis, then managing director of the London agency Mather & Crowther. By 1963 Ogilvy, Benson & Mather billed $55m across 19 clients, Rolls-Royce among them. Time called him “the most sought-after wizard in today’s advertising industry” in 1962, and he is widely called the father of advertising.

misattribution.heading: How it travels
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with this one. What drops away is everything Ogilvy put underneath it.

items.why: In the book the sentence is a heading, and the case for it follows immediately: You wouldn’t tell lies to your own wife. Don’t tell them to mine. Do as you would be done by. Quoted on its own it reads as a taste test; with its three sentences attached it is an argument about lying to strangers.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Ogilvy’s own, in his own book. Quote Investigator ↗ cites Confessions of an Advertising Man, chapter 5, page 99.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Ogilvy wrote Confessions of an Advertising Man in 1963, when his agency was fifteen years old and billing $55m across nineteen clients. Wikipedia ↗ describes the book as an eleven-chapter playbook of more than two hundred rules; this is the one that turns a commercial question into a domestic one.

The move is the test, not the sentiment. Ogilvy does not argue that honest advertising performs better — he asks the writer to picture a specific reader, his own wife, and then points out that the reader on the other side of the page is somebody else’s.
detailsBody: The book was originally printed in 5,000 copies, with the profit intended for Ogilvy’s son David Fairfield Ogilvy. It sold more than a million.

A note on our sourcing: we could not open the book. The Internet Archive’s scan of the 1963 Atheneum edition is lending-restricted and not full-text searchable from here, so both page numbers on this page are other people’s locators — Quote Investigator’s 99 for the Atheneum printing, Wikiquote’s 87 for the Ballantine one. They cite the same book and the same wording, and nothing we found contradicts either.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces "Never Write an Advertisement Which You Wouldn't Want Your Own Family To Read" to David Ogilvy, Confessions of an Advertising Man, chapter 5, page 99 (Atheneum, New York, 1963), and states the page was verified against a hardcopy.

Wikiquote's sourced section transcribes "Never Write an Advertisement Which You Wouldn't Want Your Own Family To Read. You wouldn't tell lies to your own wife. Don't tell them to mine. Do as you would be done by." and cites Confessions of an Advertising Man, p. 87 (Ballantine Books).

Wikipedia states Confessions of an Advertising Man is a 1963 book by David Ogilvy, published by Atheneum in August 1963, structured as an eleven-chapter playbook of more than two hundred rules, first printed in 5,000 copies and later selling more than a million.

The Internet Archive holds a scan of the 1963 Atheneum edition of Confessions of an Advertising Man; its metadata gives the publisher as Atheneum, and the item is lending-restricted so its text cannot be searched.
